Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Javier Morales was 67 when he came for treatment, a widowed Mexican American prosecutor who had spent decades in courtrooms projecting steadiness, command, and certainty. He described the assault in a restrained, exact way that matched his professional style, but the precision of his account made clear how sharply it remained with him. It had happened after an evening work function with people he knew through his professional world. He had accepted a ride and then found himself in a private setting with men who were not strangers to him, people whose names and faces were familiar enough that he had not felt he needed to guard himself. He remembered with particular force the physical sensation of the room and his skin: the unnatural coolness against his body, the way a specific temperature registered on him and seemed to freeze the moment in place. What stayed with him was not only the violation itself but the collapse of his expectation that known, respectable people were safe.

In the weeks afterward, Javier found that the memory did not behave like an ordinary recollection. It arrived without permission, cutting across his day while he reviewed case files or stood at counsel table. He said the memory was not vague or dreamlike but painfully clear, as if every visual detail had been preserved intact. At times he would be in his office and suddenly it no longer felt as though he were remembering something that had happened in the past; for a few moments it seemed to him that he was back there again, with the same exposure on his skin and the same certainty that he was trapped in a room with people he knew and could not trust. He could be preparing a witness or reading discovery and the scene would force itself into his mind so completely that he had to stop and steady himself before continuing.

Certain moments in his daily life became especially difficult. Being around children unsettled him in ways he found hard to explain out loud. In courthouse hallways, when families came in for hearings or when he passed a waiting area where children sat beside adults, he would feel an immediate tightening in his body and an urgent wish to leave. He was not afraid of the children themselves; rather, their presence seemed to make him acutely aware of innocence, vulnerability, and exposure, and from there the assault was suddenly close again. Encounters with people connected to the men involved were even more potent. If he heard a familiar surname, saw someone from the same social circle, or recognized a face linked even indirectly to that time, his body reacted before he could think. The memory was there at once, fully formed.

Over the following months, Javier’s way of moving through the world narrowed. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that danger was easiest to survive if he located it first. He avoided unfamiliar places because not knowing the layout felt intolerable; if he could not immediately judge where the exits were, who was nearby, and what could be used as a weapon, he did not feel he could protect himself. In restaurants, public buildings, and even professional conferences, he scanned exits as soon as he entered. He noticed letter openers, heavy lamps, glass bottles, and metal objects in a room with the same automatic speed other people might notice décor. At work this was woven into his day. Entering a new courtroom or a conference room in another office, he would pause just long enough to map the doors and identify anything that could be dangerous. Colleagues likely saw him as methodical. Javier knew it was more than that.

He also lived with a private sense of contamination that he found humiliating. He described feeling dirty because of what had happened, not metaphorically but with a stubborn physical reality that no amount of washing seemed to alter. Alongside that was a fixed fear that his body had been permanently damaged. He monitored physical sensations closely and interpreted them against the assault, carrying a quiet conviction that something irreversible had been done to him.

These changes cost him. Widowed already, he became more solitary. He declined invitations if the setting was unfamiliar, and his world became increasingly organized around places he believed he could assess. The discipline that made him a strong prosecutor kept him functioning, but by the time he sought help he was exhausted by how much effort ordinary days required. What brought him in was not a single crisis so much as the accumulation of moments in which he felt his life had shrunk to vigilance, intrusion, and dread. He said he wanted, at minimum, to walk into a room without first planning for violence and to be near other people—including children in ordinary public spaces—without feeling the past break over him as if it were happening again. What frightened him most was the possibility that this sense of danger and damage would be the final shape of the rest of his life.
